It was not a great while after the affair of the pipe, that one morning shortly after breakfast, Ahab, as was his wont, ascended the cabin-gangway to the deck. There most sea-captains usually walk at that hour, as country gentlemen, after the same meal, take a few turns in the garden.

Soon his steady, ivory stride was heard, as to and fro he paced his old rounds, upon planks so familiar to his tread, that they were all over dented, like geological stones, with the peculiar mark of his walk. Did you fixedly gaze, too, upon that ribbed and dented brow; there also, you would see still stranger foot-prints—the foot-prints of his one unsleeping, ever-pacing thought.

But on the occasion in question, those dents looked deeper, even as his nervous step that morning left a deeper mark. And, so full of his thought was Ahab, that at every uniform turn that he made, now at the main-mast and now at the binnacle, you could almost see that thought turn in him as he turned, and pace in him as he paced; so completely possessing him, indeed, that it all but seemed the inward mould of every outer movement.
“D’ye mark him, Flask?” whispered Stubb; “the chick that’s in him pecks the shell. ’Twill soon be out.”
The hours wore on;—Ahab now shut up within his cabin; anon, pacing the deck, with the same intense bigotry of purpose in his aspect.

It drew near the close of day. Suddenly he came to a halt by the bulwarks, and inserting his bone leg into the auger-hole there, and with one hand grasping a shroud, he ordered Starbuck to send everybody aft.
“Sir!” said the mate, astonished at an order seldom or never given on ship-board except in some extraordinary case.
“Send everybody aft,” repeated Ahab. “Mast-heads, there! come down!”

When the entire ship’s company were assembled, and with curious and not wholly unapprehensive faces, were eyeing him, for he looked not unlike the weather horizon when a storm is coming up, Ahab, after rapidly glancing over the bulwarks, and then darting his eyes among the crew, started from his standpoint; and as though not a soul were nigh him resumed his heavy turns upon the deck. With bent head and half-slouched hat he continued to pace, unmindful of the wondering whispering among the men; till Stubb cautiously whispered to Flask, that Ahab must have summoned them there for the purpose of witnessing a pedestrian feat. But this did not last long. Vehemently pausing, he cried:—
“What do ye do when ye see a whale, men?”
“Sing out for him!” was the impulsive rejoinder from a score of clubbed voices.
“Good!” cried Ahab, with a wild approval in his tones; observing the hearty animation into which his unexpected question had so magnetically thrown them.
“And what do ye next, men?”
“Lower away, and after him!”
“And what tune is it ye pull to, men?”
“A dead whale or a stove boat!”

More and more strangely and fiercely glad and approving, grew the countenance of the old man at every shout; while the mariners began to gaze curiously at each other, as if marvelling how it was that they themselves became so excited at such seemingly purposeless questions.
But, they were all eagerness again, as Ahab, now half-revolving in his pivot-hole, with one hand reaching high up a shroud, and tightly, almost convulsively grasping it, addressed them thus:—

“All ye mast-headers have before now heard me give orders about a white whale. Look ye! d’ye see this Spanish ounce of gold?”—holding up a broad bright coin to the sun—“it is a sixteen dollar piece, men. D’ye see it? Mr. Starbuck, hand me yon top-maul.”

While the mate was getting the hammer, Ahab, without speaking, was slowly rubbing the gold piece against the skirts of his jacket, as if to heighten its lustre, and without using any words was meanwhile lowly humming to himself, producing a sound so strangely muffled and inarticulate that it seemed the mechanical humming of the wheels of his vitality in him.

Receiving the top-maul from Starbuck, he advanced towards the main-mast with the hammer uplifted in one hand, exhibiting the gold with the other, and with a high raised voice exclaiming: “Whosoever of ye raises me a white-headed whale with a wrinkled brow and a crooked jaw; whosoever of ye raises me that white-headed whale, with three holes punctured in his starboard fluke—look ye, whosoever of ye raises me that same white whale, he shall have this gold ounce, my boys!”
“Huzza! huzza!” cried the seamen, as with swinging tarpaulins they hailed the act of nailing the gold to the mast.
“It’s a white whale, I say,” resumed Ahab, as he threw down the topmaul: “a white whale. Skin your eyes for him, men; look sharp for white water; if ye see but a bubble, sing out.”

All this while Tashtego, Daggoo, and Queequeg had looked on with even more intense interest and surprise than the rest, and at the mention of the wrinkled brow and crooked jaw they had started as if each was separately touched by some specific recollection.
“Captain Ahab,” said Tashtego, “that white whale must be the same that some call Moby Dick.”
“Moby Dick?” shouted Ahab. “Do ye know the white whale then, Tash?”
“Does he fan-tail a little curious, sir, before he goes down?” said the Gay-Header deliberately.
“And has he a curious spout, too,” said Daggoo, “very bushy, even for a parmacetty, and mighty quick, Captain Ahab?”

“And he have one, two, three—oh! good many iron in him hide, too, Captain,” cried Queequeg disjointedly, “all twiske-tee be-twisk, like him—him—” faltering hard for a word, and screwing his hand round and round as though uncorking a bottle—“like him—him—”

“Corkscrew!” cried Ahab, “aye, Queequeg, the harpoons lie all twisted and wrenched in him; aye, Daggoo, his spout is a big one, like a whole shock of wheat, and white as a pile of our Nantucket wool after the great annual sheep-shearing; aye, Tashtego, and he fan-tails like a split jib in a squall. Death and devils! men, it is Moby Dick ye have seen—Moby Dick—Moby Dick!”

“Captain Ahab,” said Starbuck, who, with Stubb and Flask, had thus far been eyeing his superior with increasing surprise, but at last seemed struck with a thought which somewhat explained all the wonder. “Captain Ahab, I have heard of Moby Dick—but it was not Moby Dick that took off thy leg?”

“Who told thee that?” cried Ahab; then pausing, “Aye, Starbuck; aye, my hearties all round; it was Moby Dick that dismasted me; Moby Dick that brought me to this dead stump I stand on now. Aye, aye,” he shouted with a terrific, loud, animal sob, like that of a heart-stricken moose; “Aye, aye! it was that accursed white whale that razeed me; made a poor pegging lubber of me for ever and a day!” Then tossing both arms, with measureless imprecations he shouted out: “Aye, aye! and I’ll chase him round Good Hope, and round the Horn, and round the Norway Maelstrom, and round perdition’s flames before I give him up. And this is what ye have shipped for, men! to chase that white whale on both sides of land, and over all sides of earth, till he spouts black blood and rolls fin out. What say ye, men, will ye splice hands on it, now? I think ye do look brave.”
“Aye, aye!” shouted the harpooneers and seamen, running closer to the excited old man: “A sharp eye for the white whale; a sharp lance for Moby Dick!”

“God bless ye,” he seemed to half sob and half shout. “God bless ye, men. Steward! go draw the great measure of grog. But what’s this long face about, Mr. Starbuck; wilt thou not chase the white whale? art not game for Moby Dick?”

“I am game for his crooked jaw, and for the jaws of Death too, Captain Ahab, if it fairly comes in the way of the business we follow; but I came here to hunt whales, not my commander’s vengeance. How many barrels will thy vengeance yield thee even if thou gettest it, Captain Ahab? it will not fetch thee much in our Nantucket market.”

“Nantucket market! Hoot! But come closer, Starbuck; thou requirest a little lower layer. If money’s to be the measurer, man, and the accountants have computed their great counting-house the globe, by girdling it with guineas, one to every three parts of an inch; then, let me tell thee, that my vengeance will fetch a great premium here!”
“He smites his chest,” whispered Stubb, “what’s that for? methinks it rings most vast, but hollow.”
“Vengeance on a dumb brute!” cried Starbuck, “that simply smote thee from blindest instinct! Madness! To be enraged with a dumb thing, Captain Ahab, seems blasphemous.”

“Hark ye yet again—the little lower layer. All visible objects, man, are but as pasteboard masks. But in each event—in the living act, the undoubted deed—there, some unknown but still reasoning thing puts forth the mouldings of its features from behind the unreasoning mask. If man will strike, strike through the mask! How can the prisoner reach outside except by thrusting through the wall? To me, the white whale is that wall, shoved near to me. Sometimes I think there’s naught beyond. But ’tis enough. He tasks me; he heaps me; I see in him outrageous strength, with an inscrutable malice sinewing it. That inscrutable thing is chiefly what I hate; and be the white whale agent, or be the white whale principal, I will wreak that hate upon him. Talk not to me of blasphemy, man; I’d strike the sun if it insulted me. For could the sun do that, then could I do the other; since there is ever a sort of fair play herein, jealousy presiding over all creations. But not my master, man, is even that fair play. Who’s over me? Truth hath no confines. Take off thine eye! more intolerable than fiends’ glarings is a doltish stare! So, so; thou reddenest and palest; my heat has melted thee to anger-glow. But look ye, Starbuck, what is said in heat, that thing unsays itself. There are men from whom warm words are small indignity. I meant not to incense thee. Let it go. Look! see yonder Turkish cheeks of spotted tawn—living, breathing pictures painted by the sun. The Pagan leopards—the unrecking and unworshipping things, that live; and seek, and give no reasons for the torrid life they feel! The crew, man, the crew! Are they not one and all with Ahab, in this matter of the whale? See Stubb! he laughs! See yonder Chilian! he snorts to think of it. Stand up amid the general hurricane, thy one tost sapling cannot, Starbuck! And what is it? Reckon it. ’Tis but to help strike a fin; no wondrous feat for Starbuck. What is it more? From this one poor hunt, then, the best lance out of all Nantucket, surely he will not hang back, when every foremast-hand has clutched a whetstone? Ah! constrainings seize thee; I see! the billow lifts thee! Speak, but speak!—Aye, aye! thy silence, then, that voices thee. (Aside) Something shot from my dilated nostrils, he has inhaled it in his lungs. Starbuck now is mine; cannot oppose me now, without rebellion.”
“God keep me!—keep us all!” murmured Starbuck, lowly.

But in his joy at the enchanted, tacit acquiescence of the mate, Ahab did not hear his foreboding invocation; nor yet the low laugh from the hold; nor yet the presaging vibrations of the winds in the cordage; nor yet the hollow flap of the sails against the masts, as for a moment their hearts sank in. For again Starbuck’s downcast eyes lighted up with the stubbornness of life; the subterranean laugh died away; the winds blew on; the sails filled out; the ship heaved and rolled as before. Ah, ye admonitions and warnings! why stay ye not when ye come? But rather are ye predictions than warnings, ye shadows! Yet not so much predictions from without, as verifications of the foregoing things within. For with little external to constrain us, the innermost necessities in our being, these still drive us on.
“The measure! the measure!” cried Ahab.

Receiving the brimming pewter, and turning to the harpooneers, he ordered them to produce their weapons. Then ranging them before him near the capstan, with their harpoons in their hands, while his three mates stood at his side with their lances, and the rest of the ship’s company formed a circle round the group; he stood for an instant searchingly eyeing every man of his crew. But those wild eyes met his, as the bloodshot eyes of the prairie wolves meet the eye of their leader, ere he rushes on at their head in the trail of the bison; but, alas! only to fall into the hidden snare of the Indian.

“Drink and pass!” he cried, handing the heavy charged flagon to the nearest seaman. “The crew alone now drink. Round with it, round! Short draughts—long swallows, men; ’tis hot as Satan’s hoof. It seemed as though, by some nameless, interior volition, he would fain have shocked into them the same fiery emotion accumulated within the Leyden jar of his own magnetic life. The three mates quailed before his strong, sustained, and mystic aspect. Stubb and Flask looked sideways from him; the honest eye of Starbuck fell downright.

“In vain!” cried Ahab; “but, maybe, ’tis well. For did ye three but once take the full-forced shock, then mine own electric thing, that had perhaps expired from out me. Perchance, too, it would have dropped ye dead. Perchance ye need it not. Down lances! And now, ye mates, I do appoint ye three cupbearers to my three pagan kinsmen there—yon three most honorable gentlemen and noblemen, my valiant harpooneers. Disdain the task? What, when the great Pope washes the feet of beggars, using his tiara for ewer? Oh, my sweet cardinals! your own condescension, that shall bend ye to it. I do not order ye; ye will it. Cut your seizings and draw the poles, ye harpooneers!”
Silently obeying the order, the three harpooneers now stood with the detached iron part of their harpoons, some three feet long, held, barbs up, before him.

“Stab me not with that keen steel! Cant them; cant them over! know ye not the goblet end? Turn up the socket! So, so; now, ye cup-bearers, advance. The irons! take them; hold them while I fill!” Forthwith, slowly going from one officer to the other, he brimmed the harpoon sockets with the fiery waters from the pewter.

“Now, three to three, ye stand. Commend the murderous chalices! Bestow them, ye who are now made parties to this indissoluble league. Ha! Starbuck! but the deed is done! Yon ratifying sun now waits to sit upon it. Drink, ye harpooneers! drink and swear, ye men that man the deathful whaleboat’s bow—Death to Moby Dick! God hunt us all, if we do not hunt Moby Dick to his death!” The long, barbed steel goblets were lifted; and to cries and maledictions against the white whale, the spirits were simultaneously quaffed down with a hiss. Starbuck paled, and turned, and shivered. Once more, and finally, the replenished pewter went the rounds among the frantic crew; when, waving his free hand to them, they all dispersed; and Ahab retired within his cabin.

What, when the great Pope washes the feet of beggars, using his tiara for ewer? Oh, my sweet cardinals! your own condescension, _that_ shall bend ye to it. I do not order ye; ye will it. Cut your seizings and draw the poles, ye harpooneers!”
Silently obeying the order, the three harpooneers now stood with the detached iron part of their harpoons, some three feet long, held, barbs up, before him.

“Stab me not with that keen steel! Cant them; cant them over! know ye not the goblet end? Turn up the socket! So, so; now, ye cup-bearers, advance. The irons! take them; hold them while I fill!” Forthwith, slowly going from one officer to the other, he brimmed the harpoon sockets with the fiery waters from the pewter.

“Now, three to three, ye stand. Commend the murderous chalices! Bestow them, ye who are now made parties to this indissoluble league. Ha! Starbuck! but the deed is done! Yon ratifying sun now waits to sit upon it. Drink, ye harpooneers! drink and swear, ye men that man the deathful whaleboat’s bow—Death to Moby Dick! God hunt us all, if we do not hunt Moby Dick to his death!” The long, barbed steel goblets were lifted; and to cries and maledictions against the white whale, the spirits were simultaneously quaffed down with a hiss. Starbuck paled, and turned, and shivered. Once more, and finally, the replenished pewter went the rounds among the frantic crew; when, waving his free hand to them, they all dispersed; and Ahab retired within his cabin.

modern_en.title: Chapter 36 — The Quarter-Deck
paragraphs: (Enter Ahab: Then, all.)

It was not long after the affair of the pipe that one morning shortly after breakfast, Ahab, as usual, climbed the cabin gangway to the deck. There most sea captains usually walk at that hour, the way country gentlemen take a turn in the garden after the same meal.

Soon his steady, ivory stride could be heard as he paced back and forth on his old rounds, over planks so familiar to his step that they were dented all over, like geological stones, with the distinctive marks of his walk. If you stared fixedly at his ribbed and dented brow, you would see still stranger footprints there — the footprints of his one sleepless, ever-pacing thought.

But on this particular occasion, those dents looked deeper, just as his nervous step that morning left a deeper mark. Ahab was so full of his thought that at every regular turn he made — now at the mainmast, now at the binnacle — you could almost see that thought turn inside him as he turned, and pace inside him as he paced. It possessed him so completely, in fact, that it all but seemed the inner mold of every outward movement.
"Do you notice him, Flask?" whispered Stubb. "The chick inside him is pecking at the shell. It'll be out soon."
The hours wore on — Ahab now shut up in his cabin, then pacing the deck again, with the same intense, fanatical purpose in his face.
The day was drawing to a close. Suddenly he stopped by the bulwarks, inserted his bone leg into the auger-hole there, and with one hand gripping a shroud, he ordered Starbuck to send everyone aft.
"Sir!" said the mate, astonished at an order seldom or never given on a ship except in some extraordinary situation.
"Send everybody aft," repeated Ahab. "Mastheads, there! Come down!"

When the entire ship's company was assembled and, with curious and somewhat uneasy faces, was watching him — for he looked not unlike the windward horizon when a storm is coming up — Ahab, after glancing quickly over the bulwarks and then darting his eyes among the crew, left his post. As though no one were near him, he resumed his heavy pacing across the deck. With bent head and half-slouched hat, he continued to pace, ignoring the wondering whispers among the men, until Stubb cautiously whispered to Flask that Ahab must have assembled them to witness some kind of walking performance. But this didn't last long. Pausing forcefully, he cried:
"What do you do when you see a whale, men?"
"Sing out for him!" was the instant answer from a score of voices in unison.
"Good!" cried Ahab, wild approval in his voice, as he watched the hearty excitement his unexpected question had so magnetically stirred in them.
"And what do you do next, men?"
"Lower away, and after him!"
"And what tune do you pull to, men?"
"A dead whale or a stove boat!"

Stranger and fiercer grew the glad, approving look on the old man's face with every shout. Meanwhile, the sailors began glancing curiously at each other, as if marveling at how they themselves had become so excited by such seemingly pointless questions.
But they were all eagerness again as Ahab, now half-revolving in his pivot-hole, one hand reaching high up a shroud and gripping it tightly, almost convulsively, addressed them:

"All you masthead-standers have already heard me give orders about a white whale. Look here! Do you see this Spanish gold ounce?" — holding up a broad, bright coin to the sun — "It's a sixteen-dollar piece, men. Do you see it? Mr. Starbuck, hand me that top-maul."

While the mate went for the hammer, Ahab, without speaking, slowly rubbed the gold piece against the skirts of his jacket, as if to heighten its shine. Without using any words, he hummed softly to himself, making a sound so strangely muffled and unclear that it seemed like the mechanical humming of the wheels of his vitality inside him.

Taking the top-maul from Starbuck, he advanced toward the mainmast with the hammer raised in one hand and the gold coin displayed in the other, and in a loud, raised voice he cried: "Whichever of you spots me a white-headed whale with a wrinkled brow and a crooked jaw — whichever of you spots me that white-headed whale with three holes punctured in his starboard fluke — look here, whichever of you spots me that same white whale, he shall have this gold ounce, my boys!"
"Hurrah! Hurrah!" cried the seamen, swinging their tarpaulin hats as they cheered the act of nailing the gold to the mast.
"It's a white whale, I say," Ahab continued, throwing down the hammer. "A white whale. Keep your eyes peeled for him, men. Watch for white water. If you see so much as a bubble, sing out."

All this time, Tashtego, Daggoo, and Queequeg had been watching with even more intense interest and surprise than the rest. At the mention of the wrinkled brow and crooked jaw, they had each started as if individually touched by some specific memory.
"Captain Ahab," said Tashtego, "that white whale must be the same one some call Moby Dick."
"Moby Dick?" shouted Ahab. "Do you know the white whale, then, Tash?"
"Does he spread his tail a little strangely, sir, before he dives?" said the Gay Header deliberately.
"And does he have an unusual spout, too," said Daggoo, "very bushy, even for a sperm whale, and very quick, Captain Ahab?"

"And he have one, two, three — oh! many many iron in him hide, too, Captain," cried Queequeg in his broken way, "all twiske-tee be-twisk, like him — him —" struggling for the word and screwing his hand round and round as if uncorking a bottle — "like him — him —"

"Corkscrew!" cried Ahab. "Yes, Queequeg, the harpoons lie all twisted and wrenched in him. Yes, Daggoo, his spout is a big one, like a whole sheaf of wheat, and white as a pile of our Nantucket wool after the great annual sheep-shearing. Yes, Tashtego, and he fans his tail like a split jib in a squall. Death and devils! Men, it is Moby Dick you have seen — Moby Dick — Moby Dick!"

"Captain Ahab," said Starbuck, who with Stubb and Flask had been watching his superior with growing surprise but now seemed struck by a thought that somewhat explained the wonder, "Captain Ahab, I have heard of Moby Dick — but it was not Moby Dick that took off your leg?"

"Who told you that?" cried Ahab. Then, pausing: "Yes, Starbuck. Yes, my hearties, all of you. It was Moby Dick that dismasted me. Moby Dick that brought me to this dead stump I stand on now. Yes, yes!" he shouted with a terrible, loud, animal sob, like that of a heart-stricken moose. "Yes, yes! It was that accursed white whale that razeed me — cut me down like a warship sheared of its upper deck — and made a poor peg-legged lubber of me forever and a day!" Then, throwing both arms wide, with measureless curses he shouted: "Yes, yes! And I'll chase him around the Cape of Good Hope, and around the Horn, and around the Norway Maelstrom, and around the flames of hell before I give him up. And this is what you have signed on for, men! To chase that white whale on both sides of land, and over all sides of earth, until he spouts black blood and rolls fin out. What do you say, men — will you splice hands on it now? I think you look brave."
"Yes! Yes!" shouted the harpooners and seamen, running closer to the excited old man. "A sharp eye for the white whale! A sharp lance for Moby Dick!"

"God bless you," he seemed to half sob and half shout. "God bless you, men. Steward! Go draw the great measure of grog. But what's this long face about, Mr. Starbuck? Won't you chase the white whale? Aren't you game for Moby Dick?"

"I'll face his crooked jaw, and the jaws of Death too, Captain Ahab, if it fairly comes in the way of the business we're here for. But I came here to hunt whales, not my commander's vengeance. How many barrels will your vengeance yield you, even if you get it, Captain Ahab? It won't fetch you much in our Nantucket market."

"Nantucket market! Ha! But come closer, Starbuck — you need to go a layer deeper. If money is to be the measure, man, and the accountants have computed their great counting-house, the globe, by girdling it with guineas, one to every three parts of an inch — then let me tell you that my vengeance will fetch a great premium here!"
"He strikes his chest," whispered Stubb. "What's that for? It seems to ring vast, but hollow."
"Vengeance on a dumb animal!" cried Starbuck. "That simply struck you from blindest instinct! Madness! To be enraged with a mindless creature, Captain Ahab, seems blasphemous."

"Listen again — the deeper layer. All visible things, man, are nothing but cardboard masks. But in each event — in the living act, the undeniable deed — there, some unknown but still reasoning thing puts forth the molded shape of its features from behind the unreasoning mask. If a man would strike, strike through the mask! How can the prisoner reach outside except by thrusting through the wall? To me, the white whale is that wall, shoved close against me. Sometimes I think there's nothing beyond it. But that's enough. He tasks me. He heaps me. I see in him outrageous strength, with an inscrutable malice giving it sinew. That inscrutable thing is chiefly what I hate. And whether the white whale is the agent or the principal, I will wreak that hate upon him. Don't talk to me of blasphemy, man — I'd strike the sun if it insulted me. For if the sun could do that, then I could do the other, since there is always a kind of fair play in this, with jealousy presiding over all creation. But not even that fair play is my master, man. Who is over me? Truth knows no boundaries. Take your eyes off me! More unbearable than a fiend's glare is a dull, stupid stare! So, so — you flush red and go pale. My heat has melted you into an angry glow. But listen, Starbuck — what is said in heat unsays itself. There are men from whom hot words are only a small indignity. I didn't mean to provoke you. Let it go. Look! See those Turkish cheeks of spotted tawny brown — living, breathing pictures painted by the sun. The pagan leopards — the heedless, unworshipping things that live and seek and give no reasons for the torrid life they feel! The crew, man, the crew! Aren't they one and all with Ahab in this matter of the whale? See Stubb — he laughs! See that Chilean — he snorts just thinking of it. Stand up against the general hurricane? Your one tossed sapling cannot, Starbuck! And what is it? Think about it. It's only helping to strike a fin — no great feat for Starbuck. What more is it? From this one poor hunt, then, the best lance out of all Nantucket will surely not hang back, when every common sailor has already grabbed a whetstone? Ah! Compulsions seize you — I see it! The wave lifts you! Speak — speak! Yes, yes! Your silence, then — that speaks for you. (Aside) Something shot from my flaring nostrils, and he has breathed it into his lungs. Starbuck is mine now. He cannot oppose me now without rebellion."
"God keep me! — keep us all!" murmured Starbuck, quietly.

But in his joy at the mate's enchanted, silent consent, Ahab did not hear his ominous prayer. Nor the low laugh from the hold. Nor the foreboding vibrations of the wind in the rigging. Nor the hollow flap of the sails against the masts, as for a moment their hearts sank in. For again Starbuck's downcast eyes lit up with the stubbornness of life. The subterranean laugh died away. The winds blew on. The sails filled out. The ship heaved and rolled as before. Ah, you warnings and omens! Why don't you stay when you come? But rather than warnings, you are predictions — you shadows! Yet not so much predictions from outside as confirmations of what was already inside. For with little to restrain us from without, the deepest necessities within our being still drive us on.
"The measure! The measure!" cried Ahab.

Receiving the brimming pewter mug and turning to the harpooners, he ordered them to produce their weapons. Then, lining them up before him near the capstan with their harpoons in hand, while his three mates stood at his side with their lances and the rest of the crew formed a circle around the group, he stood for a moment searching every man's face. Those wild eyes met his the way the bloodshot eyes of prairie wolves meet the eye of their leader before he rushes ahead of the pack on the trail of the buffalo — but alas, only to fall into the hidden trap of the Indian.

"Drink and pass!" he cried, handing the heavy, full flagon to the nearest seaman. "The crew alone drinks now. Pass it round! Short sips — long swallows, men. It's hot as Satan's hoof. Good, good — it goes round well. It spirals into you. It forks out at the serpent-snapping eye. Well done — nearly drained. That way it went, this way it comes. Hand it back — here's a hollow! Men, you are like the years: brimming life is gulped and gone. Steward, refill!"

"Listen now, my brave ones. I have gathered you all around this capstan. You mates, flank me with your lances. You harpooners, stand there with your irons. And you, stout sailors, ring me in, so I may in some fashion revive a noble custom of my fisherman fathers before me. O men, you will yet see that — Ha! Boy, back already? Bad pennies don't come back any sooner. Hand it here. Why, now, this pewter would have run brimming again if you weren't such a St. Vitus' imp — away with you, you shaking fever!"

"Advance, you mates! Cross your lances before me. Good! Let me touch the center." So saying, with extended arm he grasped the three level, radiating lances at their crossed center point. As he did so, he suddenly and nervously twitched them, meanwhile looking intently from Starbuck to Stubb, from Stubb to Flask. It seemed as though by some nameless, inner force of will, he wanted to shock into them the same fiery emotion stored in the Leyden jar of his own magnetic life. The three mates quailed before his strong, sustained, mystic presence. Stubb and Flask looked sideways away from him. The honest eye of Starbuck fell straight to the deck.

"In vain!" cried Ahab. "But maybe that's for the best. For if you three had once taken the full-forced shock, then my own electric thing might perhaps have drained out of me. Perhaps, too, it would have dropped you dead. Perhaps you don't need it. Lower lances! And now, you mates, I appoint you three cupbearers to my three pagan kinsmen there — those three most honorable gentlemen and noblemen, my valiant harpooners. You disdain the task? What — when the great Pope washes the feet of beggars, using his tiara for a water jug? Oh, my sweet cardinals! Your own condescension — that will bend you to it. I don't command you — you will it. Cut your lashings and draw the poles, you harpooners!"
Silently obeying the order, the three harpooners now stood holding the detached iron tips of their harpoons, about three feet long, barbs pointing up, before him.

"Don't stab me with that sharp steel! Tilt them — tilt them over! Don't you know the goblet end? Turn up the socket! Good, good. Now, you cupbearers, step forward. The irons! Take them. Hold them while I fill!" Then, slowly going from one officer to the next, he filled the harpoon sockets to the brim with the fiery liquor from the pewter.

"Now, three to three, you stand. Present the murderous chalices! Hand them over, you who are now partners in this unbreakable league. Ha! Starbuck! — but the deed is done! That ratifying sun now waits to set its seal on it. Drink, you harpooners! Drink and swear, you men who man the deadly whaleboat's bow — Death to Moby Dick! God hunt us all if we do not hunt Moby Dick to his death!" The long, barbed steel goblets were raised. To cries and curses against the white whale, the spirits were gulped down together with a hiss. Starbuck paled, turned, and shuddered. Once more, and finally, the refilled pewter went the rounds among the frenzied crew. Then, as he waved his free hand to them, they all dispersed, and Ahab retired to his cabin.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 36 — Agterdækket
paragraphs: (Ahab kommer ind: Så alle.)

Der gik ikke længe efter pibe-episoden, før Ahab en morgen kort efter morgenmaden som sædvanlig steg op ad kahytstrappen til dækket. Der plejer de fleste skibsførere at gå frem og tilbage på det tidspunkt, ligesom landlige godsejere tager en tur i haven efter samme måltid.

Snart kunne man høre hans faste skridt af elfenben, mens han travede frem og tilbage på sin gamle runde, over planker, der var så vant til hans trin, at de var fyldt med mærker af hans gang, ligesom geologiske sten. Stirrede man fast på hans furede og buklede pande, ville man se endnu mærkeligere fodspor der — sporene efter hans ene søvnløse, evigt travende tanke.

Men netop denne gang så mærkerne dybere ud, ligesom hans nervøse skridt den morgen satte et dybere præg. Ahab var så fuld af sin tanke, at man ved hver regelmæssig vending, han tog — nu ved stormasten, nu ved kompashuset — næsten kunne se tanken vende sig inde i ham, når han vendte sig, og travle inde i ham, når han travede. Den besatte ham faktisk så fuldstændigt, at den næsten virkede som den indre støbeform for enhver ydre bevægelse.
»Lægger du mærke til ham, Flask?« hviskede Stubb. »Kyllingen inde i ham hakker i skallen. Den er snart ude.«
Timerne sneg sig af sted — Ahab nu indespærret i sin kahyt, så igen travende på dækket med den samme intense, fanatiske beslutsomhed i ansigtet.

Dagen var ved at gå på hæld. Pludselig standsede han ved skanseklædningen, stak sit benben ned i borehullet dér og greb med den ene hånd fat i et vant, og så befalede han Starbuck at sende alle agterud.
»Sir!« sagde styrmanden, forbløffet over en ordre, der sjældent eller aldrig gives på et skib, medmindre noget helt usædvanligt er på færde.
»Send alle agterud,« gentog Ahab. »Mastetoppene, derude! Kom ned!«

Da hele skibets besætning var samlet og med nysgerrige og noget urolige ansigter så på ham — for han lignede ikke så lidt den luvvendte horisont, når der er storm på vej — kastede Ahab et hurtigt blik ud over skanseklædningen og lod så øjnene fare ind mellem mandskabet og forlod sin plads. Som om ingen var i nærheden af ham, tog han igen sin tunge gang på tværs af dækket. Med bøjet hoved og halvt nedslået hat blev han ved at gå uden at bryde sig om det forundrede hvisken blandt mændene, indtil Stubb forsigtigt hviskede til Flask, at Ahab nok havde samlet dem for at se en slags gang-opvisning. Men det varede ikke længe. Han standsede brat og råbte:
»Hvad gør I, når I ser en hval, mænd?«
»Vi råber op efter den!« lød det øjeblikkelige svar fra tyve stemmer i kor.
»Godt!« råbte Ahab med vildt bifald i stemmen, mens han så den hjertelige begejstring, hans uventede spørgsmål så magnetisk havde vakt hos dem.
»Og hvad gør I så, mænd?«
»Firer ned og efter den!«
»Og i hvilken takt ror I, mænd?«
»En død hval eller en knust båd!«

Mere og mere mærkeligt og vildt voksede det glade, bifaldende udtryk i den gamles ansigt ved hvert råb. Imens begyndte sømændene at kigge nysgerrigt på hinanden, som om de undrede sig over, hvordan de selv var blevet så ophidsede af så tilsyneladende meningsløse spørgsmål.
Men de var alle ivrige igen, da Ahab, der nu halvt drejede sig rundt i sit hul, med den ene hånd højt oppe på et vant, som han greb om hårdt, næsten krampagtigt, talte til dem:

»I alle, som står på udkig i masterne, har allerede hørt mig give ordrer om en hvid hval. Se her! Ser I denne spanske guldunse?« — og han holdt en bred, blank mønt op mod solen — »Den er seksten dollars værd, mænd. Ser I den? Mr. Starbuck, ræk mig den der topmaul.«

Mens styrmanden hentede hammeren, gned Ahab uden at sige noget langsomt guldstykket mod skøderne på sin jakke, som for at forøge dets glans. Uden at bruge ord nynnede han sagte for sig selv med en lyd, der var så mærkeligt dæmpet og utydelig, at den lød som den mekaniske brummen fra hjulene i hans livskraft inde i ham.

Han tog topmaulen fra Starbuck og gik hen mod stormasten med hammeren løftet i den ene hånd og guldmønten fremvist i den anden, og med høj, hævet stemme råbte han: »Den af jer, der får øje på en hvidhovedet hval for mig, med en furet pande og en skæv kæbe — den af jer, der får øje på den hvidhovedede hval for mig med tre huller stukket gennem sin styrbords halefinne — se her, den af jer, der får øje på netop den hvide hval for mig, han skal have denne guldunse, mine drenge!«
»Hurra! Hurra!« råbte sømændene og svingede deres tjærede hatte, mens de jublede over, at guldet blev slået fast på masten.
»Det er en hvid hval, siger jeg,« fortsatte Ahab og smed hammeren. »En hvid hval. Hold øjnene åbne efter den, mænd. Hold udkig efter hvidt vand. Hvis I ser blot en boble, så råb op.«

Hele den tid havde Tashtego, Daggoo og Queequeg fulgt med endnu mere intens interesse og forbavselse end de andre. Da han nævnte den furede pande og den skæve kæbe, fór de alle sammen, som om hver især var blevet rørt af en bestemt erindring.
»Kaptajn Ahab,« sagde Tashtego, »den hvide hval må være den samme, som nogle kalder Moby Dick.«
»Moby Dick?« råbte Ahab. »Kender du så den hvide hval, Tash?«
»Breder den halen lidt mærkeligt ud, sir, før den dykker?« sagde Gay Head-indianeren eftertænksomt.
»Og har den også en usædvanlig blæst,« sagde Daggoo, »meget busket, selv for en kaskelot, og meget hurtig, kaptajn Ahab?«

»Og den have en, to, tre — oh! mange mange jern i sin hud, også, kaptajn,« råbte Queequeg på sit brudte sprog, »alle vrid-vri vrid, som — som —« mens han kæmpede for ordet og drejede hånden rundt og rundt, som om han trak en prop op af en flaske — »som — som —«

»Proptrækker!« råbte Ahab. »Ja, Queequeg, harpunerne ligger alle sammen vredet og vristet i den. Ja, Daggoo, dens blæst er stor, som et helt neg hvede, og hvid som en bunke af vores Nantucket-uld efter den store årlige fåreklipning. Ja, Tashtego, og den vifter med halen som en flænset klyver i et vindstød. Død og djævle! Mænd, det er Moby Dick, I har set — Moby Dick — Moby Dick!«

»Kaptajn Ahab,« sagde Starbuck, der sammen med Stubb og Flask i voksende forbavselse havde iagttaget sin overordnede, men nu syntes grebet af en tanke, der til dels forklarede undringen, »kaptajn Ahab, jeg har hørt om Moby Dick — men det var ikke Moby Dick, der tog Deres ben?«

»Hvem har fortalt dig det?« råbte Ahab. Så holdt han inde: »Ja, Starbuck. Ja, mine gutter, alle sammen. Det var Moby Dick, der tog masten fra mig. Moby Dick, der bragte mig ned på denne døde stump, jeg står på nu. Ja, ja!« råbte han med et frygteligt, højt, dyrisk hulk som fra en hjerteramt elg. »Ja, ja! Det var den forbandede hvide hval, der raserede mig — skar mig ned som et krigsskib, der er barberet for sit øverste dæk — og gjorde mig til en stakkels pælebenet landkrabbe for evigt og altid!« Så kastede han begge arme ud til siden og råbte med umådelige forbandelser: »Ja, ja! Og jeg vil jage den rundt om Kap det Gode Håb og rundt om Kap Horn og rundt om Norges malstrøm og rundt om helvedes flammer, før jeg giver den op. Og det er det, I har skrevet under på, mænd! At jage den hvide hval på begge sider af land og over alle sider af jorden, til den sprøjter sort blod og ruller finnen op. Hvad siger I, mænd — vil I give hinanden hånden på det nu? Jeg synes, I ser modige ud.«
»Ja! Ja!« råbte harpunererne og sømændene og løb tættere på den ophidsede gamle. »Et skarpt øje efter den hvide hval! En skarp lanse til Moby Dick!«

»Gud velsigne jer,« lød det, som om han halvt hulkede og halvt råbte. »Gud velsigne jer, mænd. Steward! Gå og hent den store portion grog. Men hvad er det for et langt ansigt, Mr. Starbuck? Vil du ikke jage den hvide hval? Er du ikke med på Moby Dick?«

»Jeg vil se hans skæve kæbe i øjnene og Dødens kæber også, kaptajn Ahab, hvis det ærligt kommer på tværs af det arbejde, vi er her for. Men jeg kom her for at fange hvaler, ikke for at hævne min kommandør. Hvor mange tønder vil Deres hævn give Dem, selv hvis De får den, kaptajn Ahab? Den vil ikke indbringe Dem meget på vores marked i Nantucket.«

»Marked i Nantucket! Ha! Men kom tættere på, Starbuck — du må et lag dybere ned. Hvis penge skal være målestokken, mand, og regnskabsførerne har udregnet deres store kontor, kloden, ved at omslutte den med guineas, én for hver tre fjerdedele tomme — så lad mig sige dig, at min hævn her vil indbringe en stor præmie!«
»Han slår sig for brystet,« hviskede Stubb. »Hvad skal det til for? Det lyder umådeligt, men hult.«
»Hævn over et stumt dyr!« råbte Starbuck. »Som bare ramte Dem af blindeste instinkt! Vanvid! At rase mod et sanseløst væsen, kaptajn Ahab, forekommer mig at være blasfemi.«

»Hør igen — det dybere lag. Alle synlige ting, mand, er kun pap-masker. Men i hver begivenhed — i den levende handling, den uomtvistelige gerning — dér skubber noget ukendt, men dog tænkende sit ansigts formede træk frem bag den tankeløse maske. Hvis en mand vil slå, så skal han slå gennem masken! Hvordan skulle fangen nå ud, uden at han bryder gennem muren? For mig er den hvide hval den mur, skubbet helt ind på livet af mig. Nogle gange tænker jeg, at der slet intet er bagved. Men det er nok. Han plager mig. Han tynger mig. Jeg ser i ham en ubegribelig styrke, og en uudgrundelig ondskab giver den sener. Det uudgrundelige er det, jeg mest af alt hader. Og uanset om den hvide hval er den, der handler, eller den, der står bag, vil jeg hævne mit had på ham. Tal ikke til mig om blasfemi, mand — jeg ville slå efter solen, hvis den fornærmede mig. For hvis solen kunne gøre det, så kunne jeg gøre det andet, da der altid er en slags retfærdigt spil i dette, med misundelsen som hersker over al skabelse. Men ikke engang det retfærdige spil er min herre, mand. Hvem er over mig? Sandheden kender ingen grænser. Tag øjnene fra mig! Mere uudholdeligt end en djævels glor er et sløvt, dumt stirrende blik! Sådan, sådan — du bliver rød og så bleg igen. Min hede har smeltet dig til en vred glød. Men hør, Starbuck — det, der siges i hede, tager sig selv tilbage. Der er mænd, som hede ord kun er en lille krænkelse for. Jeg ville ikke ægge dig. Lad det ligge. Se! Se de tyrkiske kinder af plettet, gulbrunt — levende, åndende billeder malet af solen. De hedenske leoparder — de ubekymrede, ugudelige væsener, der lever og søger og ikke giver nogen grunde for det brændende liv, de føler! Mandskabet, mand, mandskabet! Er de ikke alle som én med Ahab i denne sag om hvalen? Se Stubb — han ler! Se chileneren — han fnyser, bare han tænker på det. Skal man stille sig op mod den almindelige orkan? Dit ene, kastede træ kan det ikke, Starbuck! Og hvad er det egentlig? Tænk over det. Det er kun at hjælpe med at ramme en finne — ikke noget stort stykke arbejde for Starbuck. Hvad mere er det? Fra denne ene stakkels jagt skulle den bedste lanse i hele Nantucket da vel ikke holde sig tilbage, når hver eneste menige sømand allerede har grebet en slibesten? Ah! Tvang griber dig — jeg ser det! Bølgen løfter dig! Tal — tal! Ja, ja! Din tavshed, så — den taler for dig. (For sig selv) Noget skød ud af mine flammende næsebor, og han har åndet det ind i sine lunger. Starbuck er min nu. Han kan ikke modsætte sig mig nu uden at gøre oprør.«
»Gud bevare mig! — bevare os alle!« mumlede Starbuck sagte.

Men i sin glæde over styrmandens fortryllede, tavse samtykke hørte Ahab ikke hans ildevarslende bøn. Heller ikke den lave latter fra lastrummet. Heller ikke vindens uhyggelige dirren i rigningen. Ikke sejlenes hule flaben mod masterne, mens deres hjerter et øjeblik sank sammen. For endnu en gang lyste Starbucks nedslåede øjne op af livets stædighed. Den underjordiske latter døde hen. Vinden blæste videre. Sejlene fyldtes ud. Skibet løftede sig og rullede som før. Ah, I advarsler og varsler! Hvorfor bliver I ikke, når I kommer? Men snarere end advarsler er I forudsigelser — I skygger! Og dog ikke så meget forudsigelser udefra som bekræftelser af det, der allerede var indeni. For når vi har så lidt, der holder os tilbage udefra, driver de dybeste nødvendigheder i vores væsen os stadig videre.
»Målet! Målet!« råbte Ahab.

Han tog imod det fyldte tinkrus, vendte sig mod harpunererne og befalede dem at tage deres våben frem. Så stillede han dem op foran sig ved gangspillet med harpunerne i hånden, mens hans tre styrmænd stod ved hans side med deres lanser, og resten af mandskabet dannede en kreds omkring gruppen. Han stod et øjeblik og søgte i hver eneste mands ansigt. De vilde øjne mødte hans, som præriens blodsprængte ulveøjne møder øjnene på deres leder, før han styrter forrest i flokken på sporet af bøflen — men ak, kun for at falde i indianerens skjulte fælde.

»Drik og send videre!« råbte han og rakte den tunge, fyldte kande til den nærmeste sømand. »Nu drikker kun mandskabet. Send den rundt! Korte slurke — lange synk, mænd. Den er hed som Satans hov. Godt, godt — den går godt rundt. Den snor sig ind i dig. Den forgrener sig ud i det slangebidende øje. Godt gået — næsten tømt. Den vej gik den, denne vej kommer den. Giv den tilbage — her er et hul! Mænd, I er som årene: det fyldte liv bliver slugt og er væk. Steward, fyld op!«

»Hør nu, mine tapre. Jeg har samlet jer alle om dette gangspil. I styrmænd, stil jer ved min side med jeres lanser. I harpunerere, stå dér med jeres jern. Og I, stærke sømænd, slut ring om mig, så jeg på en eller anden måde kan genoplive en ædel skik fra mine fiskerfædre før mig. O mænd, I skal endnu se, at — Ha! Dreng, allerede tilbage? Dårlige skillinger kommer ikke hurtigere tilbage. Giv den hertil. Jamen, nu ville det tin have været fyldt igen, hvis du ikke var sådan en sankt Veds-djævel — væk med dig, din rystende feber!«

»Frem, I styrmænd! Kryds jeres lanser foran mig. Godt! Lad mig røre ved midten.« Med de ord greb han med strakt arm de tre vandrette, stråleformede lanser i deres krydsede midtpunkt. Idet han gjorde det, rykkede han pludselig og nervøst i dem og så imens indtrængende fra Starbuck til Stubb, fra Stubb til Flask. Det så ud, som om han ved en navnløs, indre viljekraft ville give dem det samme brændende følelsesstød, som lå oplagret i hans eget magnetiske livs leydnerflaske. De tre styrmænd veg tilbage for hans stærke, vedvarende, mystiske nærvær. Stubb og Flask så sidelæns væk fra ham. Starbucks ærlige blik faldt lige ned i dækket.

»Forgæves!« råbte Ahab. »Men måske er det til det bedste. For hvis I tre en gang havde taget det fulde stød, så var min egen elektriske ting måske løbet ud af mig. Måske ville det også have slået jer døde om. Måske har I ikke brug for det. Sænk lanserne! Og nu, I styrmænd, udnævner jeg jer tre til mundskænke for mine tre hedenske frænder dér — de tre mest ærede herrer og adelsmænd, mine tapre harpunerere. Foragter I opgaven? Hvad — når den store pave vasker tiggeres fødder og bruger sin tiara som vandkrus? Åh, mine søde kardinaler! Jeres egen nedladenhed — den vil bøje jer til det. Jeg befaler jer ikke — I vil det selv. Skær jeres surringer over og træk skafterne, I harpunerere!«
De tre harpunerere adlød tavst og stod nu foran ham med de løsnede jernspidser af deres harpuner, omkring tre fod lange, med modhagerne opad.

»Stik mig ikke med det skarpe stål! Vip dem — vip dem over! Kender I ikke bægerenden? Vend hulrummet opad! Godt, godt. Nu, I mundskænke, træd frem. Jernene! Tag dem. Hold dem, mens jeg fylder!« Så gik han langsomt fra den ene officer til den næste og fyldte harpunhulrummene til randen med den brændende drik fra tinkruset.

»Nu står I tre og tre. Fremvis de morderiske bægre! Ræk dem frem, I, som nu er partnere i dette ubrydelige forbund. Ha! Starbuck! — men gerningen er gjort! Den stadfæstende sol venter nu på at sætte sit segl under den. Drik, I harpunerere! Drik og sværg, I mænd, der bemander den dødbringende hvalbåds stævn — Død over Moby Dick! Gud jage os alle, hvis vi ikke jager Moby Dick til døde!« De lange stålbægre med modhager blev løftet. Under råb og forbandelser mod den hvide hval blev spiritusserne sunket ned sammen med en hvislen. Starbuck blev bleg, vendte sig og gøs. Endnu en gang, og for sidste gang, gik det genfyldte tin rundt blandt det rasende mandskab. Så, da han vinkede til dem med sin frie hånd, spredtes de alle, og Ahab trak sig tilbage til sin kahyt.
